title: The periodic table and its history

tips.title: Atomic number, not atomic weight
tips.body: The modern table orders by **protons**. Atomic weight **averages over isotopes**, so an element rich in a heavy isotope can outweigh the element with one more proton — which is exactly why the old ordering occasionally failed.

tips.title: Replaced against adapted
tips.body: The **nuclear model replaced** the plum pudding model — they are incompatible. **Bohr adapted** the nuclear model, adding that electrons orbit at specific distances. Using the right verb shows you know what happened.

tips.title: Gaps are predictions
tips.body: A table that only tidies known elements **cannot be tested**. A gap says an element exists and predicts its properties — so it could have been **wrong**. It was not, which is the strongest support an idea can get.

tips.title: A metal is defined chemically
tips.body: **Reacts to form positive ions.** Shiny, conducting and sitting on the left are all **consequences**. An answer defining a metal by appearance has described the evidence, not the property.

tips.title: Bohr was accepted on the numbers
tips.body: His **theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations** — not because his model was neater. Models are judged against evidence, and that is the general rule this history teaches.

why.matters:
A list of the elements would be a reference. The periodic table is something much better: a **machine for predicting**. Put the elements in order of protons and the ones with the same number of outer electrons fall into the same column, so the table tells you how an element you have never handled will behave — what charge its ion takes, what it will react with, roughly how violently.

That is also why its history is worth knowing. An arrangement that only tidies what is already known cannot be tested. One that leaves gaps can be wrong.

examples.title: The gap that had to be filled
examples.body:
Mendeleev left holes in his table rather than closing the ranks, and said what the missing elements would be like. Under silicon he described an element nobody had seen: relative atomic mass about **72**, density about **5.5 g/cm³**, forming an oxide of a particular formula.

Germanium was later dug out of a mine and measured at **72.6** and **5.32 g/cm³**. A table that merely tidied the known elements could never have done that. Predicting something that has not been found yet is how you tell an arrangement from an explanation.

examples.title: The squares that are the wrong way round
examples.body:
Order the elements by weight, as the first tables had to, and some pairs come out backwards. Tellurium is **heavier** than iodine — yet iodine plainly belongs with chlorine and bromine, and tellurium with sulfur and selenium.

Mendeleev swapped them anyway, and cobalt and nickel too, on the grounds that the chemistry mattered more than the weights, and had no way to justify it. Argon, found in 1894, needed the same swap with potassium. Ordering by **protons** justifies it exactly: a relative atomic mass is an average over isotopes, and an element rich in a heavy one can outweigh its neighbour.

visual.alt: A table of two neighbouring pairs, argon before potassium and tellurium before iodine, where the proton number rises while the relative atomic mass falls, so ordering by weight would put each pair the wrong way round

examples.title: Writing a formula without looking it up
examples.body:
The column an element sits in is the number of electrons in its outer shell, and that fixes the ion it forms. Group 1 loses one, Group 2 loses two, Group 6 gains two, Group 7 gains one — so the charges are read straight off the table.

Then the formula follows, because the charges have to cancel. Magnesium is 2+ and chlorine is 1−, so it takes two chlorines: MgCl₂. Nothing here was memorised. A wall chart and one rule give you the formula of a compound you have never met.

steps.title: How the table is arranged
steps.body:
**The elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of atomic number** — that is, in order of the number of **protons** — and **so that elements with similar properties are in columns, known as groups**.

**It is called a periodic table because similar properties occur at regular intervals.** *Periodic* means *repeating at intervals*, and that repetition is the pattern the table was built to show.

**Why elements in a group behave alike:**

> **Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, and this gives them similar chemical properties.**

That is the key sentence of the whole topic. Chemistry is decided by the **outer electrons**, so elements with the same number of them react in the same way.

- **Group 1** — one outer electron — lithium, sodium, potassium
- **Group 7** — seven outer electrons — fluorine, chlorine, bromine
- **Group 0** — a full outer shell — helium, neon, argon

**The group number tells you the outer electrons** for the main groups, which means you can read chemistry straight off the table.

**And the position tells you more than the group.** The **period** — the row — tells you how many shells are occupied. Sodium is in period 3 because its structure, 2,8,1, uses three shells.

So the table is not a list that happens to be useful. It is a **picture of electronic structure**, and every pattern in it comes from that.

steps.title: Metals and non-metals
steps.body:
The spec defines these by **what they do**, not by where they sit:

> **Elements that react to form positive ions are metals. Elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.**

That is a **chemical** definition, and it is the one to give if asked. Shininess and conductivity are consequences, not the definition.

**Where they are:**

- **The majority of elements are metals.**
- **Metals** are found to the **left** and towards the **bottom** of the periodic table.
- **Non-metals** are found towards the **right** and **top**.

**Why the position follows from the electrons.** An element on the left has **few** outer electrons, so **losing** them is the easy route to a full outer shell — and losing electrons makes a **positive** ion, which is what makes it a metal. An element on the right has **many** outer electrons, so **gaining** a few is easier than losing seven — and gaining electrons makes a **negative** ion.

So the metal–non-metal divide running down the table is not a convention. It is the line where losing electrons stops being easier than gaining them.

**Typical properties**, which follow from the bonding:

- **Metals**: shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, generally high melting points, form **basic** oxides.
- **Non-metals**: dull, poor conductors (carbon as graphite is the famous exception), brittle when solid, often low melting points, form **acidic** oxides.

steps.title: How the model of the atom developed
steps.body:
**New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.** That sentence is the point of this section — the story is the evidence for it.

**The sequence, in order:**

1. **Before the discovery of the electron**, atoms were thought to be **tiny spheres that could not be divided**.
2. **The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model**: the atom is a **ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it**.
3. **The alpha particle scattering experiment** gave results leading to the conclusion that the **mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre** — the **nucleus** — and that the **nucleus was charged**. **This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.**

   **Why the evidence forced the change.** Positive alpha particles were fired at a thin gold foil. **Most passed straight through**, so most of the atom is empty space. **Some were deflected**, so there is a concentrated positive charge that repels them. **A very few bounced back**, so almost all the mass sits in that tiny centre. A plum pudding, with its positive charge spread through the whole atom, could not turn a single particle round.
4. **Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model** by suggesting that **electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances**. **His theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations**, which is why the adaptation was accepted.
5. **Later experiments** led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be **subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge**. These were named **protons**.
6. **The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence for neutrons** within the nucleus — **about twenty years after the nucleus was accepted**.

**Two details that earn marks and are easily missed:**

- **Bohr's model was accepted because his calculations agreed with observations.** Not because it was neater. A model is accepted when it **matches the evidence**.
- **The neutron came last, and late** — roughly twenty years after the nucleus. So for two decades the nucleus was known to exist without its full contents being known.

**What the story is really teaching** is how science works: a model is held until evidence contradicts it, and then it is **changed or replaced**. The plum pudding model was not stupid — it fitted everything known at the time. The alpha scattering results were what it could not survive.

steps.title: How the periodic table developed
steps.body:
**Before the discovery of protons, neutrons and electrons, scientists attempted to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights.**

That was the only ordering available — you can weigh an element without knowing what is inside it — and it very nearly worked.

**Where it went wrong.** **The early periodic tables were incomplete, and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups if the strict order of atomic weights was followed.** Two problems, and they have different causes:

- **Incomplete**, because many elements had not yet been discovered.
- **Wrong groups**, because atomic weight is not quite the right ordering.

**What Mendeleev did.** He **overcame some of the problems** in two ways:

1. He **left gaps for elements that he thought had not been discovered**.
2. He **changed the order** in some places, rather than following atomic weights strictly.

**Why that was bold.** Leaving a gap is a **prediction**: it says an undiscovered element exists, and — because its group gives its properties — roughly what it will be like. Changing the order is stronger still: it says the data is right but the ordering principle is not quite.

**And he was vindicated.** **Elements with properties predicted by Mendeleev were discovered and filled the gaps.** A prediction that could have failed did not, which is the strongest kind of support a scientific idea can get.

**The explanation came much later.** **Knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct.** An element's atomic weight is an average over its isotopes, so an element with a lot of a heavy isotope can outweigh the element that follows it in proton number. Ordering by **atomic number** — protons — has no such problem, and that is how the table is arranged today.

**So Mendeleev was right for a reason he could not have known.** He had the correct order without the explanation, and the explanation arrived decades later.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Atomic number, not atomic weight.** The modern table is ordered by **protons**. That is the single most important correction in its history, and the reason the anomalies vanished.

**Why atomic weight misleads, in one sentence.** An element's atomic weight is an **average over its isotopes**, so an element with a high proportion of a heavy isotope can weigh more than the element with one more proton. Ordering by a quantity that averages over isotopes will occasionally invert two neighbours; ordering by proton count cannot.

**Mendeleev's gaps were predictions, and that is why they matter.** A classification that merely tidies what is known cannot be tested. One that says *an element belongs here, and it will behave like this* can be **wrong** — and when the missing elements turned up with the predicted properties, the idea gained the strongest support available. A question asking why leaving gaps was important is asking about **testable prediction**, not about neatness.

**Distinguish adapting a model from replacing it.** The nuclear model **replaced** the plum pudding model, because the two are incompatible. Bohr **adapted** the nuclear model, adding that electrons orbit at specific distances. Using the right verb shows you understand what happened.

**The plum pudding model was not foolish.** It accounted for everything known when it was proposed: atoms are neutral and contain electrons. It failed on **one experiment** — alpha scattering — which it could not explain. That is how models are meant to work, and saying so is a stronger answer than treating earlier scientists as mistaken.

**Bohr was accepted because the numbers agreed.** His **theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations**. That is the spec's own reason, and it is the general rule: models are judged against evidence.

**The neutron arrived about twenty years after the nucleus.** Worth remembering as a date-free fact, because it shows that even an accepted model can be **incomplete** for a long time without being wrong.

**And the definition of a metal is chemical.** *Forms positive ions.* Position, shine and conductivity are consequences. An answer defining a metal by its appearance has described the evidence rather than the property.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Elements are arranged in order of **atomic number** — the number of **protons**.
- Elements with **similar properties** are in columns called **groups**.
- It is **periodic** because **similar properties occur at regular intervals**.
- Elements in the same group have the **same number of outer electrons**, which gives them **similar chemical properties**.
- The **period**, or row, tells you how many **shells** are occupied.
- **Metals react to form positive ions**; **non-metals do not**.
- **Most elements are metals.** Metals are **left and bottom**; non-metals are **right and top**.
- Metals lose their **few** outer electrons; non-metals gain to fill their **many**.
- **Atom model**: indivisible spheres → **plum pudding** (after the electron) → **nuclear model** (after **alpha scattering**) → **Bohr**, with electrons at **specific distances** → **protons** → **Chadwick's neutron**, about **twenty years** after the nucleus.
- The nuclear model **replaced** the plum pudding model; Bohr **adapted** the nuclear model.
- **Bohr was accepted because his calculations agreed with observations.**
- **Periodic table history**: ordered by **atomic weight** → incomplete, and some elements in the **wrong groups** → **Mendeleev left gaps** and **changed the order** → the gaps were **filled by elements with the predicted properties** → **isotopes** explained why atomic weight was not always right.
- Atomic weight is an **average over isotopes**, which is why it can invert two neighbours.
- **New experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced.**

questions.prompt: Describe how the model of the atom developed, and explain what this shows about how science works.
questions.solution: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided. The discovery of the electron showed that atoms contain smaller negatively charged particles, and this led to the plum pudding model, in which the atom was pictured as a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it. This model accounted for everything known at the time, since it explained both that atoms are neutral overall and that they contain electrons. The results of the alpha particle scattering experiment could not be explained by it, however, because they led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre in a nucleus and that this nucleus is charged. The nuclear model therefore replaced the plum pudding model. Niels Bohr then adapted the nuclear model rather than replacing it, by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, and this adaptation was accepted because his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations. Later experiments showed that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles of equal charge, which were named protons, and about twenty years after the nucleus had been accepted the experimental work of James Chadwick provided evidence for the existence of neutrons within it. What this shows about science is that new experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced. Earlier models were not foolish but were the best account of the evidence available, and a model is accepted when its predictions agree with observation and abandoned when evidence contradicts it.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The sequence:**

1. **Before the electron** — atoms were **tiny spheres that could not be divided**.
2. **The discovery of the electron** led to the **plum pudding model**: a **ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded** in it.
3. **Alpha particle scattering** led to the conclusion that the **mass is concentrated at the centre** in a **charged nucleus**. The **nuclear model replaced** the plum pudding model.
4. **Bohr adapted** the nuclear model: **electrons orbit at specific distances**. Accepted because his **theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations**.
5. **Protons** — the nucleus's positive charge is a whole number of identical particles.
6. **Chadwick** provided evidence for the **neutron**, about **twenty years** after the nucleus was accepted.

**What it shows.** *New experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced.*

**The point that earns the top band:** the plum pudding model was **not foolish**. It explained everything known — that atoms are neutral and contain electrons — and failed on **one experiment** it could not account for. A model is accepted when it matches the evidence and abandoned when evidence contradicts it. Note also the difference between **replacing** a model and **adapting** one.

questions.prompt: Explain how the periodic table developed, and why Mendeleev's decision to leave gaps was so important.
questions.skill: the history of the periodic table
questions.solution: Before protons, neutrons and electrons had been discovered, scientists attempted to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights, since weight was the only property that could be measured without knowing what an atom contained. These early periodic tables had two problems. They were incomplete, because many elements had not yet been discovered, and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups if the strict order of atomic weights was followed. Mendeleev overcame some of these problems in two ways. He left gaps for elements that he thought had not yet been discovered, and in some places he changed the order rather than following atomic weights strictly. Leaving gaps was scientifically important because it turned a classification into a prediction. A table that merely tidies the elements already known cannot be tested, but a gap asserts that an undiscovered element exists and, because the group determines the properties, predicts approximately what that element will be like. Such a prediction could have been shown to be wrong. In the event, elements with the properties Mendeleev had predicted were discovered and filled the gaps, which is the strongest kind of support a scientific idea can receive. His decision to change the order was bolder still, because it claimed that the data were reliable but the ordering principle was not quite correct. The explanation arrived only much later, when knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct. An element's atomic weight is an average over its isotopes, so an element with a high proportion of a heavy isotope can outweigh the element with one more proton. The modern table is ordered by atomic number instead, and the anomalies disappear.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The sequence:**

1. Elements were ordered by **atomic weight**, the only property measurable without knowing what an atom contained.
2. Two problems: the tables were **incomplete**, and some elements sat in **inappropriate groups** if the strict weight order was followed.
3. **Mendeleev left gaps** for undiscovered elements, and **changed the order** in places.
4. **The gaps were filled** by elements with the properties he had **predicted**.
5. **Knowledge of isotopes** finally explained why the weight order was not always right.

**Why the gaps mattered — this is the heart of the question.** A table that merely **tidies** what is known **cannot be tested**. A gap **asserts that an undiscovered element exists** and, since the group determines the properties, **predicts what it will be like**. That prediction **could have failed**. It did not — which is the strongest support a scientific idea can receive.

**Changing the order was bolder still**: it claimed the **data were right but the ordering principle was not**.

**And the explanation came decades later.** Atomic weight is an **average over isotopes**, so an element rich in a heavy isotope can outweigh the element with **one more proton**. The modern table orders by **atomic number**, and the anomalies vanish — so Mendeleev was right for a reason he could not have known.

examTechnique.body:
Say the modern table is ordered by atomic number, not atomic weight.

Explain group similarity through the number of outer electrons.

Define metals and non-metals by whether they form positive ions.

Give the stages of the atomic model in order, and name the evidence that prompted each.

Use replaced for the nuclear model and adapted for Bohr's contribution.

Say Bohr was accepted because his calculations agreed with observations.

Explain Mendeleev's gaps as testable predictions that were later confirmed.

Explain the atomic weight anomaly by saying atomic weight averages over isotopes.
examinerErrors: Saying the modern table is ordered by atomic weight.
Writing that Bohr replaced the nuclear model.
Defining a metal by shininess or conductivity rather than by forming positive ions.
Describing earlier models as simply wrong rather than as fitting the evidence of the time.
Giving the stages of the atomic model out of order.
Saying Mendeleev left gaps to make the table look tidier.
Attributing the neutron to the alpha scattering experiment.
Explaining group similarity by position rather than by outer electrons.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the history as evidence about how science works rather than as a list of names. It says the plum pudding model fitted everything known until one experiment it could not explain, distinguishes adapting a model from replacing it, and knows Bohr was accepted because his calculations matched observation. On the periodic table it explains Mendeleev's gaps as testable predictions that could have failed, and can say precisely why atomic weight misleads: it averages over isotopes, so it will occasionally invert two neighbours, which ordering by proton count cannot do.
